objectives: Distinguish conductive, sensorineural, and mixed hearing loss by mechanism and audiogram.
Recognize signatures of presbycusis, noise-induced loss, and ototoxicity, including the 4-kHz notch.
Apply the Weber and Rinne tuning-fork tests to localize a hearing loss.

slides.title: Conductive, sensorineural, and mixed loss
slides.body:
Hearing loss is first classified by **where in the auditory pathway** the problem sits, because the location determines both the audiogram pattern and the treatment. The three categories are **conductive**, **sensorineural**, and **mixed**.

**Conductive hearing loss** arises when sound is blocked or attenuated on its way through the **outer** or **middle** ear before it ever reaches the cochlea. The sensory cells are intact; the energy simply does not get to them efficiently. Causes include a **cerumen** plug, **otitis media** (middle-ear fluid, the most common cause in children), a perforated tympanic membrane, disruption of the ossicular chain, and **otosclerosis**, an abnormal bony fixation of the **stapes** footplate. On the audiogram the hallmark is an **air-bone gap**: thresholds measured by **air conduction** (through the whole system) are worse than thresholds measured by **bone conduction** (a vibrator on the mastoid that drives the cochlea directly, bypassing the outer and middle ear). Because the cochlea works, bone-conduction thresholds stay near normal while air-conduction thresholds drop, and the vertical gap between the two curves measures the conductive component. Many conductive losses are medically or surgically correctable.

**Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL)** arises from damage to the **cochlea** (most often the **hair cells**, especially **outer hair cells**) or to the **auditory nerve**. Here there is **no air-bone gap**: both air and bone conduction are reduced together and track each other, because the problem lies *past* the conductive apparatus. SNHL is by far the most common permanent hearing loss and is generally not surgically reversible; it is managed with amplification or, when severe, cochlear implants. Typical causes are aging, noise, ototoxic drugs, genetic conditions, and viral infections.

**Mixed hearing loss** is exactly what it sounds like: a conductive component superimposed on a sensorineural one, so both air and bone conduction are reduced *and* an air-bone gap remains. A classic example is a patient with age-related SNHL who also develops middle-ear fluid. Reading these patterns is a core clinical skill, and the **air-bone gap** is the single most useful feature: present means a conductive element, absent means pure sensorineural. Two centuries of work, from **Jean-Marc Itard's** early observations through **Adam Politzer**, a founder of modern **otology** in 19th-century Vienna, to today's calibrated audiometers, refined this into the routine classification an audiologist makes at the first appointment.

slides.title: Common sensorineural pathologies
slides.body:
Most sensorineural loss falls into a handful of recognizable patterns, and recognizing the pattern often reveals the cause.

**Presbycusis** is **age-related hearing loss**, the most prevalent sensory deficit of older adults. It develops gradually and **symmetrically** and characteristically affects **high frequencies first**, producing an audiogram that **slopes downward** toward 8 kHz. The mechanism is multifactorial: loss of **outer hair cells** (sensory presbycusis), degeneration of the **stria vascularis** that maintains the endocochlear potential (metabolic or strial presbycusis, described by **Harold Schuknecht** in his classic typology), and loss of spiral ganglion neurons (neural presbycusis). Because high frequencies carry consonant information, patients say they can *hear* speech but cannot *understand* it, especially in noise, a hallmark complaint.

**Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL)** comes from prolonged or intense sound exposure that mechanically and metabolically exhausts and kills hair cells. Its signature is the **4-kHz notch** (sometimes 3-6 kHz): a localized dip in thresholds around **4000 Hz** with relative recovery at 8 kHz, giving a distinctive notched shape. The notch sits there because of the ear-canal resonance near 3-4 kHz and the basal vulnerability of that cochlear region. Early NIHL may begin as a **temporary threshold shift** that recovers after the exposure stops, but repeated insults cause a **permanent threshold shift**. Importantly, modern work by **Sharon Kujawa** and **M. Charles Liberman** (2009) revealed **cochlear synaptopathy**, or *hidden hearing loss*, in which noise destroys synapses between inner hair cells and nerve fibers even when the audiogram looks normal, degrading hearing in noise. NIHL is one of the few entirely **preventable** causes, through hearing protection and exposure limits set by bodies such as **NIOSH** and **OSHA**.

**Ototoxicity** is hair-cell or nerve damage caused by drugs and chemicals. The major culprits are **aminoglycoside antibiotics** (gentamicin, tobramycin), the chemotherapy drug **cisplatin**, **loop diuretics** (furosemide), and high-dose **aspirin/salicylates** (whose effect is usually reversible). Aminoglycosides and cisplatin preferentially destroy basal outer hair cells, again hitting high frequencies first, and monitoring audiometry during such treatment lets clinicians adjust dosing before speech frequencies are harmed.

**Tinnitus**, the perception of sound (ringing, buzzing, hissing) without an external source, accompanies many of these conditions. It is usually not a disease in itself but a symptom generated by maladaptive **central** plasticity after the loss of normal cochlear input, the brain turning up its gain and generating phantom activity. Affecting a large share of adults, tinnitus is managed with sound therapy, hearing aids, and **cognitive behavioral therapy** rather than a cure. Recognizing whether tinnitus is **pulsatile** (possibly vascular and warranting imaging) or **non-pulsatile** is an early triage step.

slides.title: The Weber and Rinne tuning-fork tests
slides.body:
Long before electronic audiometers, clinicians localized hearing loss with a simple **tuning fork**, and these bedside tests remain in daily use because they are fast and require no electricity. The standard fork is **512 Hz**: low enough to give a long-lasting tone, high enough not to be felt as mere vibration. Two tests, the **Weber** and the **Rinne**, are interpreted together. They are named for **Ernst Heinrich Weber** and **Heinrich Adolf Rinne**, 19th-century German physicians.

The **Weber test** places a vibrating fork on the **midline** of the skull, usually the forehead or the top of the head, and asks the patient where they hear the tone, left, right, or center. In a **normal** person, or in someone with **symmetric** loss, the sound is heard in the **middle**. The illuminating cases are asymmetric. In a **conductive** loss, the sound **lateralizes toward the affected (worse) ear**. This counterintuitive result occurs because the blocked outer/middle ear no longer admits competing ambient air-conducted noise, and the occlusion lets the bone-conducted tone resonate more efficiently on that side, so the bad ear actually hears the bone-conducted fork louder. In a **sensorineural** loss, the sound **lateralizes toward the better (normal) ear**, because the impaired cochlea perceives the bone-conducted tone as fainter.

The **Rinne test** compares **air conduction (AC)** with **bone conduction (BC)** in *one ear at a time*. The clinician holds the vibrating fork on the **mastoid** bone (bone conduction) until the patient can no longer hear it, then immediately moves it next to the **ear canal** (air conduction) and asks whether it is audible again. In a **normal** ear, **air conduction is better than bone conduction** (AC > BC), called a **positive Rinne**, because the efficient middle-ear amplifier makes the air route superior. In a **conductive** loss the middle-ear advantage is lost, so **bone conduction is heard longer or louder than air** (BC > AC), a **negative Rinne**, the cardinal sign of a conductive problem in that ear. In a **sensorineural** loss both routes are reduced together, so air conduction is still better than bone (Rinne stays positive, AC > BC), just at a softer overall level.

Reading them together is the trick. Suppose a patient's Weber lateralizes to the **left** ear. If the left Rinne is **negative** (BC > AC), the left ear has a **conductive** loss, the Weber went to the bad-but-occluded ear. If instead the left Rinne is **positive** and the *right* ear shows reduced thresholds, the picture points to a **right sensorineural** loss pulling the Weber toward the better left ear. These elegant logical tests, validated against the full **pure-tone audiogram**, let a clinician form a hypothesis about conductive versus sensorineural loss in under a minute, exactly the distinction that the **air-bone gap** later confirms on the audiogram.

question.question: On an audiogram, what single feature most clearly distinguishes a **conductive** from a **purely sensorineural** hearing loss?
options: A downward slope toward the high frequencies.
An **air-bone gap**: air-conduction thresholds are worse than bone-conduction thresholds in conductive loss, whereas in sensorineural loss air and bone conduction are reduced together with no gap.
question.explanation: Bone conduction bypasses the outer and middle ear and tests the cochlea directly. In conductive loss the cochlea is fine, so bone-conduction thresholds are near normal while air-conduction thresholds are poorer, leaving an air-bone gap. In sensorineural loss the deficit is in the cochlea or nerve, so both routes drop together and there is no gap. A high-frequency slope and a 4-kHz notch describe specific sensorineural patterns, and tinnitus is nonspecific.

hints: Bone conduction drives the cochlea directly, skipping the conductive apparatus.
Look for a vertical separation between the air and bone curves.
slides.workedSolution: The air-bone gap is the key. Because bone conduction tests the cochlea directly, a conductive lesion leaves bone thresholds near normal while air thresholds worsen, opening a gap. A sensorineural lesion lowers both air and bone conduction equally, so no gap appears. The notch and slope are subtypes of sensorineural patterns and tinnitus is nonspecific.

question.question: A factory worker with a notched audiogram.
question.prompt: A 45-year-old who has worked 20 years on a stamping line without hearing protection has an audiogram that is near normal at 250 to 2000 Hz, dips sharply to 55 dB HL at 4000 Hz, and recovers to 35 dB HL at 8000 Hz, bilaterally and symmetrically, with no air-bone gap. Explain what type of loss this is, what the dip at 4000 Hz is called and why it occurs there, and whether this damage was preventable.

question.question: A patient has a **negative Rinne** in the left ear (bone conduction heard longer than air conduction) and the **Weber lateralizes to the left**. What does this combination indicate?
options: A sensorineural loss in the left ear.
A conductive hearing loss in the left ear: the negative Rinne shows bone beats air on that side, and the Weber lateralizing to the worse-but-occluded left ear is the expected conductive pattern.
A sensorineural loss in the right ear.
question.explanation: A negative Rinne (BC > AC) signals a conductive loss in the tested ear, here the left. In conductive loss the Weber lateralizes toward the affected ear because occlusion enhances bone conduction and removes masking noise on that side. Both findings agree on a left conductive loss. A sensorineural loss would give a positive Rinne and a Weber that lateralizes to the better ear.

hints: Negative Rinne (BC > AC) is the cardinal sign of a conductive loss in that ear.
In conductive loss the Weber goes toward the bad ear.
slides.workedSolution: Negative Rinne means bone conduction beats air conduction in the left ear, the signature of a conductive loss there. Conductive losses pull the Weber toward the affected ear because the occluded ear hears the bone-conducted tone better. Both tests therefore agree: a left-sided conductive hearing loss.

question.question: An ear has an air-conduction threshold of **45 dB HL** and a bone-conduction threshold of **10 dB HL** at 1000 Hz. What is the **air-bone gap** in dB at that frequency?
question.hint: The air-bone gap is air-conduction threshold minus bone-conduction threshold.

question.question: Monitoring a patient on cisplatin.
question.prompt: A patient is starting chemotherapy with cisplatin and you are asked to monitor for ototoxicity. Knowing which part of the cochlea this drug damages first and which frequencies are encoded there, explain what early audiometric change you would watch for, why high-frequency monitoring above 8 kHz can catch damage before everyday speech is affected, and what the team might do if a threshold shift appears.
